one_liner: Google's Java transpiler with a WasmGC backend (J2Wasm); Sheets reports its calc worker about 2x faster than J2CL's JavaScript output.
what_it_does: J2CL transpiles Java source to Closure-style JavaScript and, through its experimental J2Wasm backend, to WasmGC modules that use the browser's garbage collector. You build with Bazel rules (j2wasm_application), get a .wasm plus JS glue, and call it from JavaScript via JsInterop; JUnit tests can run under Wasm. It is a different output target for the same Java code, not a drop-in for an existing JS bundle's API.
how_it_is_fast: Java objects become WasmGC structs and arrays with static types, so the engine skips JavaScript's dynamic property and shape checks, and Java long maps to native 64-bit integers instead of the goog.math.Long objects the JS backend uses (docs/semantics.md). The optimized rule runs Binaryen wasm-opt in three stages of repeated -O3 with --closed-world, --traps-never-happen, --gufa (whole-program flow analysis), --unsubtyping, --type-merging, itable merging and J2CL-specific passes; the V8 team measured wasm-opt making J2Wasm builds of Box2D, DeltaBlue, RayTrace and Richards 1.9x faster on average. At run time V8's speculative inlining of indirect calls (about 30% on the Sheets calc engine) and Wasm deoptimization (up to 7%, Chrome M137) supply the virtual-call devirtualization a JVM would do.
when_to_use: A large, CPU-bound Java codebase (spreadsheet formula engines, parsers, layout or business logic) already shared between server and web through J2CL, where the JavaScript build is measurably slower than the JVM.
Compute that runs in a web worker with coarse-grained calls across the JS boundary, so interop cost stays small relative to the work.

Code heavy in Java long arithmetic or tight object-oriented loops: the JS backend boxes long into goog.math.Long objects, while Wasm has native 64-bit integers (inference from docs/semantics.md, not separately measured).
Targets limited to current Chromium-based browsers (WasmGC from Chrome 119) where you can afford a Bazel plus Binaryen build.
when_not_to_use: Code that is chatty with the DOM or JS APIs, or relies on JS-native regex and string machinery: the Sheets team had to swap the Wasm-compiled re2j for the browser's RegExp to fix regex speed (snippet only).
You need Java reflection, Enum.valueOf, java.net or a complete JRE: J2CL emulates only a subset (docs/limitations.md).
Non-Bazel or Windows-native toolchains: the workflow is Bazel-only and not supported on Windows (use WSL).

You need stable, cross-browser production support guarantees: the README calls Wasm support 'work-in-progress' and the project 'alpha release for developer preview'; the 2x figure is reported only for desktop Chrome and Edge.
Small or startup-dominated workloads, where module compile and tier-up time count more than steady-state throughput (not measured in any public source seen).

integration.dependencies: Bazel (Bazelisk), Binaryen wasm-opt (third_party:binaryen), J2CL's JRE emulation
integration.min_toolchain: Bazel with the j2cl rules; browser with WasmGC (Chrome 119+ per docs) and Wasm exception handling (enabled in every wasm-opt stage)
integration.platforms: Browsers and JS engines with WasmGC; build on Linux/macOS (Windows via WSL only)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same Java source as the J2CL JavaScript build, but a different artifact (wasm module plus JsInterop glue) and a stricter browser floor

gotchas: The optimized j2wasm_application sets jre.checks.checkLevel=MINIMAL and jre.checkedMode=DISABLED and always passes Binaryen --closed-world --traps-never-happen, so code that would trap or depends on Java runtime checks (bounds, casts, nulls) can behave differently between the _dev and optimized builds.

The JS baseline differs semantically too: it maps long to goog.math.Long objects, float to 64-bit doubles and skips array bounds checks (docs/semantics.md, docs/limitations.md), so part of the gap is representation cost rather than compiler quality.
Wasm-specific JRE bugs have occurred, e.g. HashMap.computeIfAbsent with a null key threw under Wasm (issue #199, fixed 2023-08-15).

The speedup is shared credit: the speculative-inlining figures in V8's posts are V8 engine work (about 30%, not the record's unconfirmed 40%), and the 1.9x is Binaryen's, measured against unoptimized J2Wasm output rather than against JavaScript.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick J2CL's Wasm backend when the code is Java; the closest siblings do the same JS-to-WasmGC switch for other languages: Kotlin/Wasm for Kotlin, the Scala.js WebAssembly backend for Scala, and wasm_of_ocaml for OCaml. None of them gives a reproducible JS-versus-Wasm harness either, so choose by source language, not by the headline numbers.
verified_claims_summary: Google's web.dev case study (not reachable here; snippets only) says the Sheets calculation worker, Java compiled by J2CL, ran more than 3x slower as JavaScript than on the JVM, the first WasmGC build was about 2x slower than the JS build, and the tuned WasmGC build ended about 2x faster than JS in desktop Chrome and Edge; no hardware, Chrome version or method is given, and Wasm would still be about 1.5x the JVM's time (derived from the snippet figures). The V8 blog (opened via its GitHub source) adds first-party measurements: wasm-opt speeds J2Wasm builds of four Octane-style benchmarks by 1.9x on average, and speculative inlining is worth about 30% on the Sheets calc engine.
status_note: Actively developed (8,654 commits, last commit 2026-10-11), Apache-2.0 and in production in Google Sheets, but the Wasm backend is labelled experimental and the repo publishes no benchmark results, so the evidence stays first-party.
